title: Why A Beautifully Designed Classroom Is A Bad Idea
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Reacting to the Pinterest-and-Instagram trend of elaborately decorated classrooms, Linsin argues that chasing a picture-perfect room is counterproductive. He identifies four costs: it creates a self-imposed pressure to always look impressive; it consumes time and energy better spent on lesson planning and mental preparation; it often costs teachers their own money for no real instructional benefit; and most of the decor — interactive calendars, sugary mottoes, organizational systems — does nothing to improve learning. He is careful to say color and an attractive room are fine if done without stress, but he draws a sharp line between decoration and good teaching, warning that cutesy, whimsical design is frequently a red flag rather than a sign of quality instruction. His alternative vision is a spartan, museum-like room — clean, uncluttered, with open space to move — that itself communicates to students that excellence is expected.
points: Elaborately decorated 'Pinterest classrooms' create self-imposed pressure and perfectionism that can wear teachers down.
Time spent designing and maintaining a decorative classroom is time taken from lesson planning and mental preparation.
Spending personal money on classroom decor is unnecessary and does nothing to improve learning.
Most classroom decor — organizational systems, interactive calendars, motivational mottoes — adds no real instructional value.
A clean, uncluttered, nearly spartan room communicates that excellence is expected more effectively than elaborate decoration does.
quotes: You lock yourself into a prisonous state of always having to measure up, be impressive, and have the most beautiful classroom in the school. It isn’t healthy.
Good teachers sit and think before and after school. If you’re doing more physical than mental preparation, then you’re not going to be ready to teach .
You don’t have to spend your own money to be an effective teacher. It’s not part of the job and does nothing to improve learning. Stop it, really.
If it doesn’t save time or simplify your life, if isn’t absolutely needed, if you’re only doing it because your rival or friend or favorite influencer does it, then throw it out.

But never fall into the trap of believing that adorable, magical, and whimsical design, cutesy creative organization, or lamps and bean bag chairs have anything to do with good teaching. Mostly, they’re a giant red flag.
To be most effective, your classroom should be pin-neat. It should be clean and lack clutter. It should have wide-open spaces and walkways to move and breathe.
